summary: Help 5-6 year-olds experience that a push or pull is a force one thing does to another that can start, stop, speed up, slow down, or turn an object, and that a bigger push makes a bigger change. From rest, a push strong enough to move a free object such as a ball starts it moving in the direction it is pushed, while a sideways tap on an already-moving ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes. Centre real hands-on play with objects, predict-then-do comparisons that vary one thing at a time, and begin to attribute stopping to a push-back from the ground/air (friction) rather than a force 'running out'. Screen or picture activities act as complements and light checks, not replacements for physical play.
misconceptions: Only living/animate things can push or pull (a table or wall can't exert a force).
There is only a force if you can see movement — a push that doesn't visibly move something 'isn't a force'.
Impetus seed: a moving object has 'force' or 'go' stored inside it that gradually runs out, which is why it stops (MOSART; RESPeCT Grade 3).
Force is the same as the object's energy / a property the object owns, rather than an interaction between two objects.
A bigger push makes something go faster and faster forever (constant push → ever-increasing or fixed speed confusion, in seed form).

activities.title: Flick-and-push play: feel a bigger push make a bigger change
steps: Push and pull real objects (balls, toy cars, trolleys, a door, a drawer) and say out loud what happened: did it start, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction?
With two identical balls at rest, tap one gently and shove the other hard at the same time; watch which travels faster and further.

With the same gentle push (for example, the same flick from the same spot), compare a heavier ball and a lighter ball of about the same size (for example, a solid rubber ball and a hollow plastic ball), and notice how far and fast each goes. The same push usually changes the lighter ball's motion more.

Push a ball from different sides and notice that, from rest, it moves off in the direction you pushed it; once it is rolling, give it a sideways tap and watch its path bend in the direction the tap pushes it.
Predict before acting: 'Which way will it go? What happens if I push harder?' Then do it and compare with your prediction.

(Optional screen companion) In a tap-and-flick play space, drag a stretchy aimer back further to push harder and release to send a ball off; set up a side-by-side 'gentle vs strong' race on identical balls and watch the hard-pushed one go faster and further.
activities.insight: A push or pull is a force that changes how an object moves; a stronger push makes a bigger change to the motion. From rest, a push strong enough to move a free object such as a ball starts it moving in the direction it is pushed, while a sideways tap on an already-moving ball bends its existing path in the direction the tap pushes.

activities.title: Compare smooth vs rough: why things stop
steps: Give one ball the same push on a smooth floor and then on a rough carpet.
Before each roll, predict which will travel further and say why.
Watch the carpet ball stop sooner and talk about what was different between the two surfaces.
Try to slow a ball that is already rolling toward you without catching it (for example, hold a cushion in its path).
activities.insight: Things slow and stop because a surface (or air) rubs against them and pushes back — friction — not because the push is used up inside the object.

activities.title: Pushes slow and turn, not just start
steps: Take a ball that is already rolling and find a way to slow it down before it arrives (hold a cushion in its path).
Give a ball that is already rolling a sideways tap and watch its path bend in the direction the tap pushes it.
Say which of these a push can do: start it, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, change its direction — and show an example of each with a real object.
activities.insight: A push or pull is the same kind of force whether it starts, speeds up, slows, stops, or turns an object; slowing and turning are the force acting, not something different.

activities.title: Name pushes and pulls around us
steps: Sort picture cards of everyday actions into PUSH and PULL (with an adult reading or audio support).
Look at a playground or home scene and point out where someone is pushing and where someone is pulling (for example, pulling a child on a swing, pushing a trolley).
For a pictured object at rest about to be pushed, point which way it will start to move.
Use the words push, pull, and force as you describe what is happening.
activities.insight: Pushes and pulls happen all around us; naming them and reading the direction of the force builds the vocabulary that supports the hands-on experiences.

checkQuestion: This ball is sitting still on the floor. If you want it to roll over to me quickly, what would you do to it — and why does doing that make it go fast instead of slow?
checkAnswer: Give it a hard/strong push in my direction. A stronger push makes it speed up more, so a hard push makes it go faster than a gentle one; the push is the force that starts it moving and sets how fast it goes.
